title: Split a String Into the Max Number of Unique Substrings
statement:
Cut the string `s` into consecutive, non-empty pieces that, read in order, rebuild `s` exactly. No two pieces may be the same string. Return the largest number of pieces such a cut can have.

A piece is any contiguous run of characters of `s`. Keeping `s` whole (one piece) is always allowed.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

With at most 16 characters there are only 2^15 ways to place the cuts, so trying them all is feasible: that is the brute force. Backtracking does the same search smarter. Grow the split one piece at a time from left to right, remember the pieces already used in a set, and refuse any piece that is already in it. When the pieces still possible cannot beat the best count found, stop exploring that branch.

## Approach

1. Keep a set `seen` of the pieces in the current partial split and the best count `best`.
2. `backtrack(start)` handles the suffix beginning at `start`. If `start` reaches the end, the split is complete: update `best` with `seen.size`.
3. Prune: even if every remaining character became its own piece, the count would be `seen.size + (s.length - start)`. If that is not more than `best`, give up on this branch.
4. Otherwise try each `end` after `start`: the next piece is `s.slice(start, end)`. Skip it if it is already in `seen`; else add it, recurse from `end`, and remove it again.
5. Return `best` after `backtrack(0)`.

## Example 1, step by step

For `s = "ababccc"`, the search first takes `"a"`, `"b"`, then `"a"` is already used, so the third piece becomes `"ab"`. Next comes `"c"`; another `"c"` is used, so it takes `"cc"`, reaching the end with `seen = {a, b, ab, c, cc}` and `best = 5`. Every later branch is pruned or completes with at most 5 pieces, so the answer is `5`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · 2^n) in the worst case: up to 2^(n-1) cut patterns, each piece costing O(n) to slice and hash.
- Space: O(n²) characters at most for the set and O(n) recursion depth.

## Pitfalls

- Remove the piece from `seen` after the recursive call, or later branches see stale pieces.
- The last piece must also be unique; the loop includes `end === s.length`, which handles it like any other piece.
- Do not cut greedily into the shortest new piece: `"aba"` greedily gives `a, b` and then `a` is stuck, so the search must be able to undo choices.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seen` | pieces used in the current partial split |
| `best` | most pieces in any complete split found so far |
| `start` | index where the next piece begins |
| `end` | index just after the candidate piece |
| `piece` | the candidate substring `s.slice(start, end)` |

narration.3: No complete split has been counted yet.
narration.5: backtrack(start) tries every way to cut the rest of s, beginning at index start.
narration.6: Reaching the end of s means the current pieces form a complete split.
narration.7: Its piece count is the size of the set; keep the larger count.
narration.10: Even if every remaining character were its own piece, could this branch beat best?

narration.14: The candidate piece runs from start up to (not including) end.
narration.15: A piece already in the split would repeat, which is not allowed.
narration.16: Skip it and try a longer piece.
narration.18: Use the piece in the current split.
narration.19: Cut the rest of the string after this piece.
narration.20: Undo the choice so the next candidate starts from a clean set.
narration.24: Start the search with the whole string still to cut.
narration.25: Return the most pieces any valid split reached.
